street_smart.title: A group of strangers shows up at your workplace, accuses you or a colleague of some personal 'moral' violation, and starts getting aggressive — echoing a recent incident where 12 people were arrested for a violent moral-policing attack at a Bengaluru factory. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: Real incident in today's news: 12 people held for a violent moral-policing attack inside a Bengaluru factory (The Times of India).
street_smart.situation: The group is getting louder and more physical, workplace security hasn't stepped in yet, and everyone nearby is either watching or backing away. What you do in the next minute matters most.

choices.text: Move toward a secure or crowded area, alert factory security/HR immediately, and call 100 with your exact location and a description of the group.
choices.feedback: Correct. Vigilante 'moral policing' groups have no legal authority over anyone's personal choices. Getting to safety and looping in security and police fastest is what actually de-escalates the situation and creates an official record — which is exactly what led to arrests in the real case.

choices.text: Try to reason with the group and explain or justify your personal choices to calm them down.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. These groups aren't looking for a factual explanation — engaging on their terms signals you owe them an answer, and it can escalate rather than de-escalate. You don't need to justify personal choices to a mob.

choices.text: Start filming the confrontation on your phone and post it live to social media before doing anything else.
choices.feedback: Documentation matters, but not before your own safety — get clear of the group first. Visibly filming an already-agitated crowd can also provoke them further; factory CCTV and a police report are safer ways to create a record.

choices.text: Quietly leave once it's over and don't report it, to avoid further trouble.
choices.feedback: Staying silent lets the group act again unchecked — the 12 arrests in the real case only happened because the attack was reported. File a complaint at the nearest police station or call 100 even after the fact.

takeaways: Moral-policing or vigilante groups have no legal authority over your personal choices — you don't owe them an explanation.
Call 100 or your nearest police station immediately during or after such a confrontation; workplaces are expected to have a security/HR escalation protocol you can invoke.

If you're threatened over a relationship or personal choice, you can also approach the local police or the Karnataka State Commission for Women for protection, and get any injuries or threats documented via a medical or police report as soon as possible.

quiz.question: In India's parliamentary system, who formally has the power to summon and prorogue sessions of Parliament?
options: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
quiz.why: The President exercises this power on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers, reflecting India's system of a nominal head of state acting on elected government's advice.

quiz.question: Which gas do plants primarily absorb from the air during photosynthesis?
quiz.why: Plants use carbon dioxide along with water and sunlight to produce glucose and release oxygen as a by-product — the reverse of what animals do when they respire.
